item.title: Comparing the real-world effectiveness of oral corticosteroids and antifungals for the treatment of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in cystic fibrosis
item.description:
Background: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a complication of cystic fibrosis (CF) that often requires treatment. Oral corticosteroids (OCS) are the first-line therapy; however, antifungals alone or in combination with OCS are commonly used despite limited data supporting their role.

Research question: What factors are associated with antifungal treatment initiation for ABPA in people with CF? Do antifungals, with or without OCS, improve respiratory outcomes compared to OCS alone?

Study design and methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of people with CF with first diagnosis of ABPA from 2006 to 2022. Factors associated with antifungal initiation following ABPA diagnosis were evaluated using a Cox proportional hazards (PH) model. We used an inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) generalized estimating equations (GEE) model to evaluate changes in lung function before and after initiation of first treatment (OCS, antifungals, or combination treatment). IPTW Cox PH models were used to evaluate associations between the first treatment type and time to first pulmonary exacerbation and ABPA clinical relapse.

Results: Among 3,096 people with CF and incident ABPA, 74.3% received OCS and/or antifungals. Older age, CFTR modulator use, and CF liver disease were associated with longer time to antifungal initiation, while prior pulmonary exacerbations, larger care center size, and OCS use were associated with earlier initiation. OCS monotherapy was associated with an increase in forced expiratory volume in one second percent predicted slope of 0.24 (95% CI 0.09-0.38, p<0.01) after treatment initiation. No significant differences were observed between combination therapy or antifungal monotherapy compared to OCS alone in changes in lung function decline, time to pulmonary exacerbations or time to clinical relapse.

Interpretation: Combination OCS/antifungal therapy was not associated with greater improvements in lung function or reduced risk of pulmonary exacerbations or clinical relapse compared to OCS monotherapy.

item.title: Association of Antifibrotic Dosing Patterns With Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis in Real-World Data Sources
item.description:
Background: Antifibrotic therapies nintedanib and pirfenidone slow lung function decline in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). However, both medications are often poorly tolerated, leading to dose reductions and discontinuations in practice.

Research question: How do antifibrotic dose changes (reductions or cessations) affect disease progression in IPF?

Study design and methods: This retrospective study analyzed data for patients with IPF who initiated antifibrotic therapy using two US data sources: the multicenter Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry (Registry) and Duke University Health System electronic health records (EHR). Antifibrotic dose groups were defined as full dose, reduced dose for ≥3 months, or stopped therapy for ≥3 months. Associations between antifibrotic dose group, a time-varying exposure, and IPF progression, defined as composite ≥10% decline in ppFVC, all-cause hospitalization, lung transplant, or death, were analyzed by Cox proportional-hazards models adjusted for demographics and lung function.

Results: Over a median (25th/75th percentile) follow-up of 30.0 (17.5/30.0) months in the Registry and 14.0 (7.4/29.6) months in the EHR, 347/545 (63.7%) and 609/1,027 (59.3%) patients remained on full dose, respectively. Event rates for progression per 100 person-years in patients on full dose, reduced dose, or discontinuation were 39.74, 46.62, and 70.69, respectively, in the Registry and 44.82, 40.46, and 41.72 in the EHR. Time to progression did not differ significantly between patients who reduced or stopped antifibrotics and those who remained on full dose in the Registry (HR 1.17 [95% CI 0.90-1.52] for dose reduction, 1.51 [1.04-2.18] for discontinuation; P=.073) and EHR (HR 0.87 [0.69-1.09], 0.94 [0.66-1.36]; P=.476), respectively.

Interpretation: Among patients with IPF, antifibrotic dose reductions and discontinuations were common, likely due to poor drug tolerability. Disease progression occurred in a substantial proportion of patients in both cohorts, regardless of antifibrotic dosing strategy, highlighting the ongoing need for more effective and better-tolerated IPF therapies.

item.title: Optimization of Pharmacist Medication Management and Mortality in the Intensive Care Unit
item.description:
Background: Medication-related morbidity due to inappropriate prescribing, delays in appropriate treatment, and adverse drug events contributes to ICU patient mortality. Comprehensive medication management (CMM) is a care standard provided by pharmacists in collaboration with the interprofessional team. Optimizing ICU pharmacist workload via the pharmacist-to-patient ratio while ensuring daily CMM may reduce mortality.

Research question: Is ICU pharmacist staffing, measured by the pharmacist-to-patient ratio and absence of CMM, associated with in-hospital mortality among critically ill adults?

Study design and methods: Adults admitted to an ICU from 64 centers (in the United States, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia) were enrolled in a multicenter observational study that collected patient and team staffing data from August 2023-January 2025. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. The primary exposure was the pharmacist-to-patient ratio calculated per patient, averaged over the ICU stay. A secondary exposure was the absence of CMM for at least 1 day of the ICU stay. Multivariable generalized estimating equations (GEE) were used to estimate associations with in-hospital mortality, accounting for clustering by center and adjusting for patient-, ICU-, and hospital-level covariates.

Results: Among 28,795 patients enrolled, the median (IQR) pharmacist-to-patient ratio was 1:17 (13-23). Each one-patient increase in the pharmacist-to-patient ratio was associated with a 1% increase in the odds of in-hospital mortality (Odds Ratio [OR] 1.01, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.00-1.01, p=0.04). Patients who did not receive pharmacist-delivered CMM for at least 1 day of the ICU stay had 20% higher odds of in-hospital mortality (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.03-1.40, p=0.02). Patients cared for at a pharmacist-to-patient ratio of 1:15.1-46 had 10% higher odds of mortality compared to those cared for at a ratio of 1:7-15 (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.00-1.22).

Interpretation: Increasing pharmacist-to-patient ratios and the absence of pharmacist CMM every day were both associated with increased in-hospital mortality.

item.title: Effect of ondansetron on respiratory drive in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome
item.description:
Background: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is often accompanied by excessive respiratory effort contributing to patient-self-inflicted lung injury. Lung inflammation leads to increased stimulation and sensitization of pulmonary vagal afferent C-fibers. Stimulation of pulmonary C-fibers by serotonin increases respiratory effort through 5-HT3 receptors. Blocking these receptors could enable safer spontaneous ventilation and mitigate the need for deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade.

Research question: Our objective was thus to evaluate the effect of ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist, on (1) the pressure-time-product (PTP) of esophageal pressure (Peso) per minute and (2) respiratory rate, tidal volume, minute ventilation and electrical activity of the diaphragm (Edi).

Methods: We performed a single-center, single-blind, non-randomized crossover trial, including adults with ARDS (Berlin criteria), ventilated > 48 hours, on pressure-support mode. Participants underwent two consecutive phases: intravenous placebo (10 mL 0.9% saline) followed, 3 hours later, by intravenous ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg; max 16 mg). We continuously recorded airway pressure, flow, Peso, and Edi tracings, comparing respiratory parameters during each 3-hour phase using mixed effect models with participant-specific random intercepts and autoregressive-residual-correlation.

Results: We enrolled ten patients and could carry the experiment in nine. Ondansetron reduced parameters of respiratory drive. Mean inspiratory PTP fell from 108 to 85 cmH2O·s·min-1, yielding a model derived mean difference of -23 cmH2O·s·min-1 (95 % confidence interval (CI95%) [-28, -18]; p<0.001). Respiratory rate (-1.7 breaths/min; CI95% [-2.0, -1.3]), minute ventilation (-1.0 L/min; CI95% [-1.1, -0.8]), peak Edi (-2.4 μV; CI95% [-2.6, -2.2]) all declined, without significant changes in tidal volume. This was accompanied by a modest rise in PaCO2 from (+3.2 mmHg; CI95% [+1.4, +5.1]; p<0.001) and a significant improvement of the PaO2:FiO2 ratio by +23 (CI95% [6, 40] p = 0.009).

Conclusions: Ondansetron reduces the respiratory drive in invasively mechanically ventilated patients with ARDS.

Cavayas YA, Caissy JA, St-Pierre M, Williams V, Albert M, Charbonney E

item.title: Comparative Short-Term Prognostic Discrimination of the 2026 AHA/ACC and 2019 ESC Risk Classifications in Hospitalized Acute Pulmonary Embolism: A Retrospective Two-Campus Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: The 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) and 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) pulmonary embolism (PE) classifications represent severity differently: AHA/ACC spans subclinical PE through cardiopulmonary failure, whereas ESC defines high risk by hemodynamic instability. Their prognostic separation is uncertain.

Research question: How do these classifications compare in mortality discrimination and identification of patients at high observed risk in hospitalized acute PE?

Study design and methods: We retrospectively studied 2,251 patients at a two-campus Chinese tertiary hospital (2013-2025). Index time was admission for community-acquired PE and symptom onset or first objective imaging for hospital-acquired PE. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality; institutionally determined PE-related mortality was post hoc. Paired DeLong tests compared ordinal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs), and AHA/ACC categories D-E defined the analysis high-risk threshold.

Results: 127 patients (5.6%) died within 30 days and 80 (3.6%) had PE-related death. Thirty-day AUCs were 0.885 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.858-0.912) for AHA/ACC and 0.763 (95% CI, 0.721-0.806) for ESC (difference, 0.122; 95% CI, 0.084-0.160; P < .001). PE-related mortality AUCs were 0.942 and 0.826, respectively (difference, 0.116; 95% CI, 0.068-0.164; P < .001). At the analysis-defined high-risk thresholds, sensitivities for PE-related death were 83.8% for AHA/ACC categories D-E and 58.8% for the ESC high-risk stratum, with specificities of 95.1% and 95.8%, respectively. Among 37 patients in AHA/ACC categories D-E but the ESC intermediate-risk stratum, 75.7% died by 30 days and 54.1% had PE-related death. Excluding AHA/ACC A and E attenuated the 30-day AUC difference to 0.112 (95% CI, 0.038-0.186).

Interpretation: Under inpatient care, the AHA/ACC categories showed greater full-spectrum ordinal separation and identified a phenotype with substantial observed mortality risk that was not classified as ESC high risk. Attenuation within the central severity range indicated that the difference was spectrum dependent.

Take home points: Study Question:How do the 2026 AHA/ACC Acute PE Clinical Categories and the 2019 ESC scheme compare for short-term mortality prognosis in hospitalized acute PE?

Results: AHA/ACC showed greater full-spectrum ordinal separation for 30-day all-cause and institutionally determined PE-related mortality and identified an ESC intermediate-risk subgroup with high early mortality, although the difference attenuated when the AHA/ACC severity extremes were removed.

Interpretation: The findings suggest that broader severity phenotyping may identify clinically important discordance while remaining limited to prognostic performance under observed care.

item.title: Biological phenotypes of alveolar injury and immune failure predict mortality in non-HIV Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: a Spanish multicentre cohort study
item.description:
Background: Non-HIV Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) carries high in-hospital mortality, yet bedside risk stratification remains limited. Admission lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and lymphocyte count are universally available and may capture two distinct pathophysiological axes (cytolytic tissue injury and failure of adaptive immune control).

Research question: Do admission phenotypes defined by LDH and lymphocyte count identify distinct in-hospital mortality risk in non-HIV PJP?

Study design and methods: Retrospective multicentre cohort of adults with EORTC/MSGERC probable or proven non-HIV PJP admitted to three hospitals (2019-2024). Admission LDH (≥400 U/L) and lymphocyte count (<700 cells/μL) defined four phenotypes (F1-F4). The primary outcome was in-hospital, all-cause mortality analysed within a competing-risks framework (live discharge as the competing event); the primary analysis was a Fine-Gray subdistribution hazards model adjusted for CURB-65 and solid-organ malignancy, with 30-day Kaplan-Meier/Cox analyses as secondary. Discrimination and calibration were internally validated by bootstrap.

Results: Seventy-eight patients were included; in-hospital mortality was 39/78 (50.0%). The 30-day cumulative incidence of death rose monotonically across phenotypes (F1 12.5%, F2 28.6%, F3 47.1%, F4 64.0%; Gray's test p=0.008). The convergent cytolytic-immunodepressed phenotype (F4) was independently associated with mortality (subdistribution hazard ratio 6.15; 95% CI 1.27-29.84), as were CURB-65 and solid-organ malignancy; intermediate phenotypes were directional but imprecise. The multivariable prediction model retained good discrimination (optimism-corrected AUC 0.88) and calibration.

Interpretation: Two universally available admission markers define an ordered mortality gradient and a high-risk convergent phenotype in non-HIV PJP, supporting early bedside risk stratification and phenotype-stratified investigation of adjunctive therapies.

Martínez de Victoria Carazo J, Arrabal EG, Zafra LG, de Salazar A, Míguez NF, Santos FA
